Meeting header: Date: 2026-02-19 15:00 PST | Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Carlos Romero (Redwood SE), Ava Kim (Hydra CTO), Liam O'Neill (Hydra ML Eng), Priya Sarker (Hydra Platform Eng)
Summary (auto): Kickoff scoping for Hydra Labs POC focused on capacity sizing, reserved GPUs with controlled burst, operational fallback policies, and benchmark plan.
---
[00:00:03] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for hopping on. Quick intros? I'm Maya, AE on the Redwood side.
[00:00:10] Ava: Hi, Ava here, CTO at Hydra. We've got Liam and Priya with us.
[00:00:13] Liam: hey, Liam.
[00:00:15] Priya: Priya, hi.
[00:00:18] Carlos: Carlos from Redwood engineering - I'll be the SE on this POC.
[00:00:25] Maya: Goal for today: align on success criteria, share workload shape, agree sizing and burst/fallback approach, and lock a timeline.
[00:00:33] Ava: Sounds good. We're trying to validate that Redwood can meet our 99th-percentile latency targets and keep costs predictable before we go enterprise.
[00:00:40] Liam: To add, our main user flow is a multi-turn assistant with 512 token avg context, peak concurrency around 180 QPS during business hours, but sustained at 30-40 QPS overnight.
[00:00:53] Priya: Plus data residency; we need audit logs for every request and KMS key control.
[00:00:58] Carlos: Yep, noted. For the POC we typically recommend a reserved GPU baseline sized for sustained throughput, with a burst pool that can spin up for headroom plus a fallback policy to a quantized model or cached prefixes when capacity hits thresholds.
[00:01:15] Ava: Can you give numbers — what does baseline vs burst look like?
[00:01:20] Carlos: Sure. With the numbers you gave — 512 token context, 30-40 sustained QPS — we'd start with a reserved pool equivalent to 4x A100-class GPUs or 6x A10x, depending on model variant. That gets you predictable throughput for the 95th-percentile. Then we suggest a burst pool of 2-3 extra GPUs for short spikes to handle 99th-percentile events.
[00:01:44] Maya: Important nuance: burst will be a lower-cost credit-backed pool with a higher per-token rate and no SLA. Fallbacks are critical: we can route to a smaller quantized model that reduces latency and cost but may change quality slightly.
[00:01:57] Liam: When you say quantized, do you mean 8-bit or 4-bit? We've seen quality drop at 4-bit for some retrieval tasks.
[00:02:04] Carlos: Mostly 8-bit for production; we offer 4-bit as last-resort. We also have prefix KV cash — sorry, cache — for repeated prompts which can dramatically reduce token compute for multi-turn.
[00:02:17] Priya: KV cash, yes. We have a lot of repeated system prompts, that would help. How does routing and fallback happen in real-time?
[00:02:25] Carlos: Policy-based routing. Example policy: if queue length > N or estimated p95 latency > 600ms, redirect new requests to quantized model; simultaneously, enable cached responses for known prefixes, and throttle non-critical routes.
[00:02:38] Ava: We need the policy to be transparent and testable. Can you provide a playbook we can run in staging?
[00:02:44] Maya: Absolutely — we'll send an operational playbook with sample policies, thresholds, and rollback steps.
[00:02:50] Carlos: For benchmarking, we'll run three phases: baseline (reserved only), burst enabled (simulate spikes), and failure-mode (force full pool exhaustion to validate fallback correctness).
[00:03:01] Liam: What load generator do you use? We can share our JMeter scripts but prefer the Redwood benchmarking harness for parity.
[00:03:08] Carlos: We use an internal harness that models token-level costs and latency with realistic token distributions; we can run it in your staging or provide Dockerized runner.
[00:03:17] Priya: Regarding security, SSO + SAML, SOC 2, and KMS are non-negotiable. Do you have SOC 2 Type II?
[00:03:25] Maya: Yes, Redwood has SOC 2 Type II and ISO attestation. We'll share the security pack; also can run a quick compliance call with our security engineer if you want.
[00:03:33] Ava: Yes please.
[00:03:35] [00:03:36] Maya: Quick success criteria check — what would signal a win?
[00:03:39] Ava: We want three things: p95 end-to-end latency under 450ms for our main route, error rate under 1% for 72h of continuous traffic, and unit cost within 20% of our internal target. Also auditability and deterministic routing behaviors.
[00:03:55] Liam: Add: model output quality within baseline eval set (BLEU/ROUGE-ish evals or our internal score).
[00:04:01] Carlos: Great. We'll instrument the benchmark to output those metrics and compare to your baseline.
[00:04:06] [00:04:07] Maya: Timeline — we're proposing 6 weeks: week 0 setup and data transfer, week 1 baseline reserved tests, week 2 burst tests and policy tuning, week 3 failure-mode and fallback validation, week 4-5 iterate, week 6 final report and pricing negotiation.
[00:04:21] Priya: That maps well to our QA window. Are there blackouts? We can give a weekend for the dry-run.
[00:04:27] Ava: We'll target the weekend of 2026-03-07 for the dry-run.
[00:04:31] Carlos: Works from our side. For the reserved pool sizing note: if you prefer a conservative start, we can reserve 6x A10x now and scale down after we collect real metrics.
[00:04:41] Liam: What's the expected p95 per 1k tokens for those GPUs?
[00:04:45] Carlos: Ballpark: 120-180ms p95 per 1k tokens on A100-class for a 7B-ish model, 250-400ms for larger 13–70B depending on attention type. We'll include model variants in the spreadsheet.
[00:04:58] Maya: Also cost tradeoff: you can keep a cheaper quantized variant always available for cold traffic. That often reduces apparent tail latency and saves on token spend.
[00:05:08] Priya: How do fallbacks affect conversational context? If we route to a smaller model mid-conversation, will context be lost?
[00:05:14] Carlos: We'll implement context compatibility — smaller model will use the last n tokens of KV cache; quality may change but we preserve conversation continuity. Also there's an option to pin canary requests to the reserved pool to protect critical user flows.
[00:05:27] Ava: Let's talk about throttling. We prefer graceful degradation (inform user of reduced capability) over hard fails.
[00:05:33] Maya: Redwood supports tiered throttling and can return semantically downgraded responses or a short human-readable fallback message. We'll include policy examples.
[00:05:41] [00:05:42] Liam: About data: we'll need to know retention rules. We have PII in prompts, so can you confirm request logs encryption and optional ephemeral logging?
[00:05:50] Maya: Logs can be stored encrypted with your KMS, or we can enable ephemeral logging for the POC. We'll document options in the security pack.
[00:05:58] Priya: Great. Also need network setup — do you support VPC peering or private endpoints?
[00:06:03] Carlos: Both. For Private POC we can do VPC peering; for hosted with limited egress we offer whitelisted egress IPs. We'll list exact steps.
[00:06:12] Ava: Ok. Anything else on benchmarking specifics?
[00:06:15] Carlos: We'll capture token-level cost, latency histograms, error types, per-route breakdown, and a small quality test suite. We'll also run a sustained 24-72h run to detect drift and GC patterns.
[00:06:27] Liam: For the 24h runs, can Redwood push metrics to our Prometheus/Datadog?
[00:06:31] Carlos: Yes, we have Prometheus exporters and Datadog integration.
[00:06:35] Maya: Alright, quick recap of deliverables: Redwood sends playbook, benchmark spreadsheet, security pack, and initial reserved + burst sizing recommendations. Hydra sends traces, access windows, and a sample eval set. Then schedule dry-run.
[00:06:49] Ava: That matches our expectations.
[00:06:52] Priya: One more question: during burst, is autoscaling instant or queued?
[00:06:57] Carlos: Burst is pre-warmed for short bursts (warm-up latency < 10s) if you request scheduled bursts; otherwise cold spin-up is ~30-90s depending on region. For SLO-sensitive flows we recommend pre-warming or keeping a small hot standby.
[00:07:12] Liam: We may have spikes from partner integrations that are 10-15s long, so pre-warm is needed.
[00:07:17] Maya: We'll include a pre-warm playbook and cost calc for reserved standby vs on-demand cold starts.
[00:07:24] [00:07:25] Carlos: OK, last part — fallback verification. We'll run chaos tests to intentionally drop reserved pool and confirm fallback correctness, plus regression checks on quality thresholds.
[00:07:36] Ava: Good. Thanks — that's thorough.
[00:07:40] Maya: Any blockers?
[00:07:43] Priya: We'll need the security pack and the list of required IAM roles so we can provision infra.
[00:07:49] Maya: Noted.
[00:07:52] [00:07:53] Maya: Alright, we'll share next steps and action items right after the call. Thanks everyone, talk soon.
[00:07:58] Ava: Thanks!
[00:08:00] (call ends)
